newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ jobs data show NZ economy lacks traction.
newsitem.headline: NZ jobs data show NZ economy lacks traction.

text.p: A sharp rise in New Zealand's unemployment rate and the stalling of job growth confirmed the economy lacked traction, economists said on Tuesday.

The unemployment rate rose from 5.9 percent in the December quarter to 6.4 percent at March 31, its highest level in two years. Employment growth fell 0.1 percent over the March quarter for an annual growth rate of 1.1 percent.
"The continued employment growth experienced since 1992 had stopped and some decline in employment is evident," Government Statistician Len Cook said.
Economists said the news backed recent weak building and retail sales data and confidence surveys showing a one-year postponement of a tax cut package halted a further growth spurt.
But while the news was bad for job seekers and the government, there was a silver lining for home owners and exporters.
No-frills bank Ergo and its fund manager parent, the Australian Mutual Provident Society, immediately cut their variable mortgage lending rate to 8.25 percent from 8.95 percent.
Ergo Managing Director Graham Meyer said the jobless numbers confirmed that lower wholesale interest rates were sustainable.
The New Zealand dollar slipped around 15 basis points in the morning to 68.68 U.S. cents while the currency Trade-Weighted Index fell to 68.23 from 68.45.
"The data was slightly weaker than expected," said First New Zealand Capital economist Jason Wong.
"It continues the run of information we've had which suggests economic growth is weak to moderate. This recovery that everyone has been expecting, the chances are very much delayed.
"The market is pricing in easier conditions and that is very much justified at this stage. The Reserve Bank is going to allow easier monetary conditions," Wong said.
Monetary conditions via wholesale interest rates and the currency have eased substantially in the last week following indications from the central Reserve Bank that it would tolerate an easing.

"The March quarter Household Labour Force survey was unambiguously good news for the inflation outlook -- positive for bonds and negative for the currency," said Bankers Trust NZ Chief Economist David Plank.

National Bank Chief Economist Adrian Orr predicted on Reuters Financial Television that the TWI could fall to 68.0 and advised traders not to be "long" in New Zealand dollars as the next phase of the easing would probably come through the TWI.
Employment Minister Peter McCardle put a positive spin on the data, saying New Zealand's jobless rate still compared well internationally.

"New Zealand can take confidence in the fact that today's 6.4 percent result still puts our official unemployment rate clearly lower than the OECD average of 7.5 percent and seventh out of 21 OECD countries with comparable surveys," McCardle said.

But opposition Labour Party employment spokesman Steve Maharey said the the rise in unemployment and fall in people in jobs spelled trouble for the government's plan to introduce a work for the dole scheme.
"Lack of jobs is the death knell for workfare schemes," Maharey said.
